name: Cruciferous vegetables for estrogen
lead: Eating cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kale, or taking supplements derived from them, is a dietary practice some men use to keep estrogen in check. The look they are after is a drier, leaner, more masculine physique: less water retention and body fat, and less chest and facial softness that high estrogen is said to bring. Lifters on forums describe it as a food-based way to nudge estrogen metabolism, especially during a cut.

The compound at the centre of the idea is indole-3-carbinol (I3C), which forms when glucobrassicin in these vegetables breaks down and is also sold as a supplement. Wikipedia says I3C and its product 3,3'-diindolylmethane (DIM) are studied for effects on how estrogen is metabolised and for anti-cancer mechanisms, with most evidence coming from animals and cell studies and human data limited and inconclusive [1][2]. DIM is sold as a dietary supplement [2].

Cruciferous vegetables are also eaten for general health reasons: an umbrella review of 41 meta-analyses found suggestive evidence of beneficial associations with gastric, lung and endometrial cancer and with all-cause mortality [3]. No human trial was found testing cruciferous vegetables for estrogen levels or physique outcomes.
infobox: Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, kale, bok choy, arugula [3]

paras: Cruciferous vegetables include cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts, all Brassica oleracea cultivars, along with bok choy, radish, watercress, arugula and mustard [3]. I3C forms when glucobrassicin breaks down; it occurs in these vegetables and is also sold as a dietary supplement [1]. When digested, I3C gives rise to DIM, which is also sold as a supplement [2].

Wikipedia describes I3C as altering estrogen metabolism toward less estrogenic metabolites, with research focused on how it changes the way estrogen is processed [1]. In one mouse study, I3C extended survival in lupus-prone mice, with the authors reasoning that I3C alters estrogen metabolism and that lupus is estrogen dependent [4]. This is animal research and was not about appearance.
Wikipedia notes that because of its effects on estrogen, testing hormone levels is advised before regular supplement use [1].

Glucosinolates in cruciferous vegetables are converted by myrosinase into isothiocyanates, which are investigated for chemopreventive effects, and the vegetables may induce enzymes involved in detoxifying carcinogens such as aflatoxin [3]. Wikipedia lists possible risks of high intake including allergies and interactions with the anticoagulant warfarin [3]. The article does not discuss estrogen [3].

On T Nation, a poster answering a thread about low estrogen asks how many vegetables the original poster eats and says cruciferous vegetables and asparagus 'can lower e2' [5]. Another poster preparing for a first bodybuilding show says he had searched for foods that inhibit aromatase to maximise his cut and shares a list from a health website [6]. In a training log thread, a poster tells a woman trying to raise her hormone panel through weight gain that cramming in as many vegetables as possible, including cruciferous ones, may not be the best approach [7].

No studies found on cruciferous vegetables for estrogen levels or physique outcomes in men. Related work on I3C consists of animal and cell studies, such as a 2009 mouse study in lupus [4]. An umbrella review examined cruciferous vegetable intake and cancer and mortality outcomes [3].

lore.intro: On T Nation, cruciferous vegetables come up in bloodwork and cutting threads as a dietary way to lower estrogen.

claims.believers: A poster in a low-estrogen bloodwork thread lists cruciferous vegetables and asparagus as foods that can lower E2 [5].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says I3C alters estrogen metabolism, with most evidence from animals and cells and human data limited and inconclusive [1]. No human trial on vegetable intake and estradiol was found.

claims.claim: Eating aromatase-inhibiting foods helps maximise a cut
claims.believers: A first-time bodybuilding competitor describes searching for foods that inhibit aromatase to get as lean as possible [6].
claims.experts: No published study was found testing food-based aromatase inhibition for physique outcomes.

claims.claim: Large amounts of cruciferous vegetables can interfere with hormone-driven goals
claims.believers: A poster tells a person trying to raise hormone levels through weight gain that heavy vegetable intake may not help [7].
claims.experts: Wikipedia's cruciferous vegetable article does not discuss estrogen; it notes possible allergy and warfarin interaction risks at high intake [3].

refs.title: Indole-3-carbinol improves survival in lupus-prone mice by inducing tandem B- and T-cell differentiation blockades

card.summary: Broccoli-family vegetables for estrogen balance via I3C; shown in animals and cells, thin in humans.
card.note: Human evidence is limited and inconclusive; supplements alter estrogen metabolism.

quick.overview:
The claim is that cruciferous vegetables, or their compound I3C, push estrogen metabolism toward less estrogenic products.

The effect is described mostly in animal and cell studies; human evidence is limited and inconclusive.
quick.mechanism: I3C, formed from glucobrassicin in these vegetables, is reported to shift estrogen metabolism toward less estrogenic metabolites [1].
quick.risks: I3C carries skin and eye irritation warnings in its chemical classification, and Wikipedia advises checking hormone levels before regular supplement use [1].

chain: Eat cruciferous vegetables rich in glucosinolates and I3C
I3C is proposed to shift estrogen metabolism
Proponents expect less estrogen-related water retention and softness, a drier look
angle.text: Men who track estrogen during cutting phases add cruciferous vegetables or I3C/DIM supplements hoping to reduce estrogen-driven softness and water retention, for a leaner, harder look. The mechanism is based on laboratory and animal research on estrogen metabolism.
